**In Praise of the Long Way Round**

I am, by training and by temperament, a person who loves a shortcut. I know which queue moves fastest at the supermarket. I take the corridor through the library instead of going around the stacks because it saves ninety seconds. I have three different routes to work memorized, ranked by time of day, and I will switch between them mid-journey if a traffic report suggests a two-minute saving. For years I thought this was a virtue. I thought efficiency was a form of respect — respect for time, for energy, for all the things I hadn’t yet done. I wore my punctuality like a badge. I answered emails in subject lines. I skim-read.

There is a particular smugness that GPS gives you. The blue dot moves neatly along the highlighted road, and the voice calmly recalculates when you err. It tells you exactly how many minutes you will be late, as if lateness were a measurable substance you could manage. I liked that voice. She was calm. She never rambled. She never got distracted by a bakery. She never stopped to look at what was written on a wall.

Then, one Tuesday in late October, the road I had taken a thousand times was closed. A water main had burst and turned the intersection into a shallow, muddy lake. A sign, handwritten on cardboard, said DETOUR. An arrow pointed down a side street I had never taken, a narrow residential road lined with plane trees and low brick houses. I sighed, audibly, in an empty car, and followed it.

It added eleven minutes to my journey. I know because the voice told me so, in a slightly disappointed tone, as if I had personally caused the flood. But in those eleven minutes I passed a baker’s who was pulling out trays of something golden and smelling faintly of cardamom, and I made a mental note to return on Saturday. I saw a child walking a very serious-looking dog in a knitted sweater. I saw a mural I had never noticed, of a whale swimming between apartment buildings, its tail brushing a rooftop. I saw an old man sweeping leaves into a perfect, impossible pile, and he waved at me as if we were neighbors.

I arrived at work late, mildly annoyed, and yet also, strangely, clearer. My head was not full of the podcast I had been listening to at double speed. It was full of the whale.

That small, involuntary detour stayed with me. It made me think about how much of my life I had organized around the premise that the straightest line between two points was the best one, and how often that premise was not just boring but wrong.

Nature, for a start, rarely goes straight. Rivers meander, and geologists will tell you they do so for extremely good reasons. A perfectly straight river is a dying river. It erodes its banks, it moves too fast, it offers no slow eddies where fish can shelter or seeds can settle. A meander creates oxbow lakes, wetlands, a whole ecology of pause and return. The river gets to the sea eventually, but it takes the scenic route because the scenic route is the one that keeps it alive.

Our own bodies are similar. Blood does not travel in highways; it branches and loops and backtracks through capillaries so fine you need a microscope to see them. The brain is even less linear. One thought leads to a memory of a song, which leads to a smell, which leads to a person you haven’t seen in ten years, who leads to a sudden understanding of something you read last week. That is not a malfunction. That is how association works. That is how insight arrives, not by marching in single file, but by wandering in from the side door while you were looking for something else entirely.

Learning, I have come to think, is the clearest example. School tried to teach me in straight lines: one unit, then the next, then the test, then forget. Each subject was fenced off from the others. But the things I actually remember, the things that changed how I think, happened on detours. I went to the library to find a book for an assignment and got lost in the 500s, in philosophy, for an hour. I started reading about bridges because we were building one in physics and ended up reading about the history of suicide nets and the engineering of suspension cables in San Francisco. None of that was on the syllabus. All of it stuck.

Now we have optimized learning even further. We have courses that promise to teach you a language in ten minutes a day, with flashcards timed to your forgetting curve. We have summaries instead of books, key takeaways instead of the slow accumulation of atmosphere that makes a book worth reading. I am not against efficiency in learning — God knows I have needed it before an exam — but I worry when we mistake the syllabus for the education. The detour is often where the education actually happens. A child who is allowed to follow a tangent about dinosaurs into a tangent about fossils into a tangent about the museum’s dusty basement is not wasting time. She is building a web. And webs hold weight that straight lines cannot.

Travel taught me the same lesson, but with my feet. For a long time I traveled like I commuted: from airport to hotel to landmark to airport, phone in hand, optimizing each transfer. Then I got properly lost in Lisbon. My phone died — actually died, not just ran low — in a neighborhood of narrow streets that all looked identical and all sloped steeply downhill toward a view I couldn’t quite reach. I wandered for forty minutes. I found a laundry hanging over an alley like flags. I found a tiny bar where a woman sang fado to three people and a cat. I found the best grilled sardines of my life, served on paper by a man who charged me half price because I had clearly made a wrong turn and he thought it was funny.

I got back to my hotel an hour later than planned, with no photos of the things I was supposed to see, and a head full of stories I hadn’t planned to collect. When I tell people about Lisbon now, I do not talk about the tram or the monastery. I talk about the cat in the bar. The cat is the trip, in a way. The rest was just getting there.

Conversation is another place where we have lost the art of the detour. We have been trained to be concise, on-message, productive. We text in short bursts. We enter meetings with agendas and leave with action items. We ask, “How are you?” and expect, “Fine, thanks, and you?” as a kind of social handshake. But friendship rarely deepens along a straight line. It deepens in tangents. It deepens when someone mentions a dream they had and you follow it for ten minutes, even though it has nothing to do with the original topic. It deepens when you are walking together and neither of you is quite sure where you are going, and you start talking about the trees and then about your childhood and then about the fear that you are becoming your parents.

There is a reason the best conversations happen on long walks, on trains, over a second cup of tea. They are not going anywhere quickly, so the mind is free to loop and return. A tangent is not a failure of focus. Often it is the point. The main road is what you thought you wanted to discuss. The detour is what you actually needed to say.

Creative work is even more stubbornly indirect. I used to think writing was about sitting down and going straight to the end. A first draft, a second draft, done. I have since learned, painfully, that the first draft is almost always a detour — a long, rambling, wrong turn through material that teaches me what the piece is not about. I write thousands of words I will delete. I follow a character down a road that leads nowhere. I research something I don’t end up using at all. And yet those deleted miles are not wasted. They compost. They make the final version possible. The straight-line version, written quickly and confidently, is almost always the shallowest one. The long way round is where the voice appears.

Careers follow the same pattern, though we pretend otherwise in graduation speeches. Almost no one I know arrived where they are by a straight route. The doctor who started as a poet. The lawyer who spent two years running a food truck. The teacher who thought she would work in finance and quit after three months because she missed the sound of a room full of kids arguing about books. We tell neat stories about these lives afterward, smoothing out the detours into a narrative of destiny. But at the time, the detours felt like failures, like lost time. Now they look like the most honest part of the story. The job you do is rarely the straight line from your degree. It is the accumulation of side quests, interests that seemed irrelevant, skills you picked up for fun. The long way is often the only way you can discover what you actually care about.

Love, if I am honest, has taught me this more than anything. The love stories we celebrate in songs and films are often presented as a straight line: meet, fall, marry, live happily ever after. Real love, as I have seen it in my own family and in the lives around me, is full of detours. People break up and get back together. They move cities for a job and stay for a person. They have children later than they planned, or not at all, or right away when they expected to wait. They get sick. They get bored and have to find each other again. My grandparents, for example, were engaged for seven years because my grandfather was sent to work in another country and the letters took months. Seven years of waiting, of detour, and they still sound, in the recordings we have of them, like they are delighted to have arrived at each other. Maybe the waiting made the arrival mean more. Maybe not. But the straight line would have been a different love entirely.

Even in the kitchen, the straight line is a lie. You cannot caramelize onions quickly without burning them. You cannot make a good stock without simmering bones for hours. A recipe will tell you “twenty minutes,” but the real work is in the pause, in the tasting and adjusting, in the moment you step away and let the dough rise. Cooking well is largely the practice of not rushing. The long way round tastes better because time has been allowed to do its chemical and emotional work. The shortcut version is technically the same dish. It is just not as good.

There is a whole economy built on the straight line now — next-day delivery, express checkout, one-click buying, instant answers. And there is real comfort in that. But there is also a quieter economy of repair and mending and keeping things, which only makes sense if you take the long way. To repair a chair instead of buying a new one is economically irrational if you only count the hour of your labor. It becomes rational when you count the history of the chair, the skill you learn, the story you get to tell about it, the landfill you spare. Craftsmen, knitters, gardeners — they all work in detours. A garden is the ultimate detour: you plant something that will not be ready for months, you weed, you wait, you lose some things to weather and pests. The straight-line version of food is the supermarket. The long way round is the tomato you grew yourself, which was probably more expensive and less perfect and utterly worth it.

Spiritual traditions have known this for centuries. A pilgrimage is not a shortcut to holiness; it is the opposite. Saints walked hundreds of miles to get to a shrine they could have prayed to at home. The Camino de Santiago is not efficient. You could fly there in two hours. People walk it for a month because the walking is the point. Even a labyrinth — which is different from a maze, because a maze is designed to confuse you and a labyrinth is designed to lead you in, slowly, by a single winding path — teaches the same thing. You follow the line, you double back on yourself, you pass close to the center and then away from it again, and eventually you arrive. The path is the prayer. The detour is the devotion.

None of this means that straight lines are bad. That would be romantic nonsense, and I am suspicious of any philosophy that only works in good weather. Sometimes you need the straight line, urgently. If someone is hurt, you do not take the scenic route to the hospital. If there is injustice, you do not meander toward a solution. If a friend is in crisis, you do not say, “Let’s explore this tangentially.” Directness can be a form of care. It can be dignity. Respecting other people’s time, saying what you mean, keeping a promise, meeting a deadline — these are not failures of imagination. They are moral acts.

Efficiency, at its best, is a kindness. It says: I will not waste your life. I will not make you sit through a three-hour meeting that could have been an email. I will not trap you in my rambling anecdote when you have somewhere to be. There is a real ethic in that. I still believe in it, even as I learn to question it.

So the question is not how to abolish shortcuts. The question is how to budget for detours. How to leave margin in a life that is scheduled to the minute. How to protect slack, the way you protect sleep. Slack is unfashionable — it looks like nothing, like waste — but it is where the unexpected, which is another word for the alive, can enter. A day with an empty hour is not an empty day. It is an open day. It allows for a conversation that runs long, a book that pulls you in, a walk that takes you somewhere you didn’t intend.

I have started practicing small detours on purpose, as a kind of training. I walk to the shop without my phone. I read the first chapter of a book I picked up randomly, even though I have a stack of “important” books waiting. I take a different route home, even if it is longer, and I try to notice one thing I have never noticed before on that street. I let a friend finish a story that is going nowhere in particular. I linger in a museum room instead of marching toward the exit. These are tiny rebellions against my own efficiency, and they feel, at first, faintly uncomfortable, like leaving a table before the dishes are cleared. But they also feel like breathing.

Perhaps the most important detour of all is the one we take from our own plans for ourselves. I had a plan, once, neat and linear, about who I would be by forty. I would have this job and live in that city and have accomplished these things. Life, politely and repeatedly, declined to follow the plan. There were detours — illness, a relationship that ended, a job I loved that disappeared, a move that was supposed to be temporary and became permanent. For a while I treated each one as a deviation that needed correcting. Now I am learning to treat them as information. They are telling me what I value. They are telling me what I can bear and what I cannot. They are, in the best sense, the curriculum.

I think we need to teach this more kindly, especially to young people who are being fed a constant diet of optimized paths. We need to tell them that getting lost is not the same as failing. That curiosity is not a distraction. That the story you tell at a dinner party will almost always be the story of the wrong turn, not the highway. That a life well-lived will have a map that looks messy and human, with loops and dead ends and places you returned to because they were good.

On that Tuesday when the road was closed, I eventually arrived where I needed to go. I was late. The voice estimated it precisely. But I also arrived somewhere else — in a slightly different mood, with a whale on my mind and a bakery I wanted to visit again. The detour did not cancel the destination. It added to it.

Maybe that is the real lesson. The long way round is not a rejection of arrival. It is a richer way of arriving. You still get there, usually. You just get there with more in your pocket — a smell, a color, a name, a conversation, a question you hadn’t thought to ask. And sometimes, if you are lucky, you realize that the way was where you were going all along.
